body.text: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk‘s recent visit to India from October 21-23 underscored the growing relations between New Delhi and Warsaw. However, while there is much to be said about the newfound momentum in ties, clear differences exist over Russia.

During the Cold War, India maintained robust relations with Central and Eastern Europe because of their shared affiliation with the Soviet Union. For example, Czechoslovakia was India’s largest trading partner in Eastern Europe, and Poland was one of India’s defense suppliers. However, in the post-Cold War era, India’s engagement with Central and Eastern Europe weakened. Instead, India devoted considerable energy and attention to Western Europe, namely the United Kingdom, France, and Germany.

However, within the past decade, New Delhi has re-engaged with Central and Eastern Europe, illustrated by India’s External Affairs Minister, S. Jaishankar’s visits to Bulgaria and Serbia in 2019, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Poland in 2024, and more recently, Modi’s visit to Slovakia and President of India Droupadi Murmu’s visit to Romania in June and July 2026, respectively. In a significant development, India took part in its first summit with members of the Visegrad Group, or V4, when Jaishankar met his Polish, Slovakian, Czech, and Hungarian counterparts at the sidelines of the UNGA in September 2026.
Tusk’s recent visit is reflective of India’s broader re-engagement with Central and Eastern Europe following the Cold War.
The key drivers of the growing Indo-Polish relationship include defense and trade.

One of India’s major goals is to diversify its arms sources away from Russia, and it has done so through greater indigenization and expanded defense partnerships, such as with France. While India’s desire to lessen reliance on Moscow predates the Ukraine War, the conflict accelerated it, such as through delayed arms deliveries, like the S-400s, and Russia’s growing dependency on China, which New Delhi fears could make Moscow unwilling or unable to sell arms to India, as during the 1962 Sino-Indian War.

As India seeks to lessen reliance on Russia, it has sought to deepen defense relations with Poland. While India’s primary security partner in Europe has traditionally been Paris, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has facilitated a continent-wide industrial rearmament. As a frontline state on Europe’s eastern flank, Poland has assumed a greater role in European security. As such, Poland’s growing importance within European security has correlated with deepening Indo-Polish defense industrial cooperation.

For example, in 2024, when the two countries upgraded their relationship to a “strategic partnership,” they announced in their 2024-2029 action plan to deepen defense industrial ties. Notably, in February 2026, the Polish ambassador to India, Piotr Antoni Świtalski, said India used Polish drones during Operation Sindoor.

Beyond defense, economic relations have also driven growth in the relationship. Poland’s economic weight within Europe has increased significantly since it joined the EU in 2004, and it is now the continent’s fastest-growing economy. These developments have correlated with greater Indo-Polish economic relations. Notably, from 2015 to 2025, bilateral trade between the two countries increased from $2.2 billion to $6.3 billion. India is the second-largest market for Polish companies within Asia.
The desire for both sides to deepen economic relations has been given greater importance amid the weaponization of economic dependencies by Washington and Beijing.

Policies such as the Trump administration’s “Liberation Day Tariffs” and China’s export controls on rare earth minerals have prompted many countries across Europe and Asia to reduce reliance on Beijing and Washington by cooperating with other “middle powers.” This is evident in the growing relationship between India and Europe. After the India-EU free trade agreement concluded in January 2026, Warsaw and New Delhi announced plans to double bilateral trade by 2030. Importantly, Poland is eager to become a gateway for Indian businesses as they seek to expand into central and eastern European markets.
Despite the growing momentum in relations between Poland and India, policy differences exist over Russia.

While Warsaw is aware of the legacy relationship between India and Russia and is eager to position itself as a reliable defense partner so India can reduce reliance on Russian arms, policy differences exist over the Ukraine War. Poland wants to use India’s close ties with Russia to bring Moscow to the negotiating table to end the war. Before landing in India, Tusk said India “could play a constructive role” in the war.

India also wants the war to end, as the longer it goes on, the more it deepens Russia’s dependency on China and harms the Indian economy, such as through energy prices. But New Delhi is not eager to play the role of a mediator. India’s reluctance to mediate in the conflict stems from its own policy against third-party intervention in the conflict it has with Pakistan over Kashmir, illustrated when Jaishankar remarked that India would not be a “dalal” like Pakistan, in reference to Islamabad’s role in the Iran-U.S. conflict.

Another reason is that India remains eager to maintain cordial relations with Russia. In a rather paradoxical manner, even as India reduces its military dependency on Russia, American tariffs, particularly those imposed for buying Russian energy, have reinforced New Delhi’s conviction to ensure good relations with Russia to avoid overdependence on the United States, such as by exploring options to deepen economic relations with Moscow.

Ultimately, even as India’s engagement with Poland has evolved from viewing Warsaw through the lens of its historical association with the Soviet bloc to engaging it through its role as an influential EU player, New Delhi is not quite ready to relinquish its longstanding historical ties with Moscow.
